The gifted Romanian writer-director Cristian Mungiu makes tense realist thrillers that lay bare his country's history of corruption and authoritarianism. In Beyond the Hills , he took aim at intolerance within the Romanian Orthodox Church. In his 2007 masterpiece, 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days , he laid bare the cruelties of the communist dictatorship in the late 1980s. That film won the Palme d'Or at Cannes and announced Mungiu as a major international talent. A few months ago, Mungiu won a second Palme d'Or for his new drama, Fjord , which, in many ways, marks something of a departure. It's his first movie shot outside Romania, but even in a fresh setting, his eye for institutional oppression and hypocrisy is as sharp as ever. Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve give superb performances as a married couple, Mihai and Lisbet Gheorghiu, who have just moved from Romania to a small town nestled among the fjords and mountains of Norway. They have five children; the oldest is in high school, the youngest still in diapers. They're also strictly observant Christians. In one scene, which features mostly English and some Romanian dialogue, they're singing hymns at home with some church friends when they get a visit from a friendly neighbor, Mia, and her teenage daughter, Noora. The townspeople are welcoming at first, and Mungiu uses wide shots and long takes to immerse us in this open, bustling community. But things get unfriendly fast for the Gheorghius. One day, a school administrator notices that their eldest daughter, Elia, has bruises on her back, and overhears her and her brother talking about having been disciplined by their parents. A call is made to Child Protective Services, and with dizzying speed, the five Gheorghiu children — including the baby — are taken away from their parents and placed in foster care. The rest of the film follows Mihai and Lisbet's efforts to get their kids back, pitting them against an unyielding Norwegian legal system. In the testimonies that emerge, we learn that one of their children had expressed anti-LGBTQ opinions in class. This raises the question of whether the Gheorghius were targeted for abusing their children, which they vehemently deny, or for refusing to adopt the progressive, secular-humanist values of their new home country. For all the acclaim and awards it's received, Fjord has proven remarkably divisive for a Mungiu movie. Although the story was inspired by a widely publicized case from 2015 , involving a Romanian Norwegian family that endured a similar ordeal, some critics have accused the film of reducing the European welfare state to a straw-man villain — an overreaching government entity that denies parents due process. Others have claimed that such responses merely prove Mungiu's point about the intolerance of the left and how tribalism and racial and religious discrimination can arise even in ostensibly inclusive communities. For my part, I found Fjord to be a blatantly yet skillfully manipulative drama that craftily withholds as much information as it reveals. Mungiu traffics in ambiguity, sometimes to the point of coyness. The episodes of alleged physical abuse are strategically obscured or kept off-screen. A plausible alternate explanation for Elia's bruises emerges, but it's never confirmed. Fascinatingly, the kids themselves never come right out and say whether they've been physically abused, and their silence on the matter feels dramatically evasive — but also, from a parent's perspective, eerily fitting. It's as if the film were saying that, with or without state interference, our children begin to become unknowable, drifting away from us, the moment they're born. I thought a lot about my own kids while watching Fjord and the outrage I'd feel if they were taken away from me. I also sifted through my complicated feelings about my own distant evangelical-Christian upbringing. Stan and Reinsve's performances, full of tightly controlled sorrow and fury, make it easy to feel for Mihai and Lisbet, and to believe that they're genuinely good, loving parents, whether or not you share the rigidity of their beliefs. And I suspect that, deep down, it's that rigidity that Mungiu takes the most issue with. It's no accident that the most sympathetic character here is that friendly neighbor, Mia, who turns out to be an attorney and agrees to represent the parents in court, noting, at one point, that she feels a moral obligation to defend the minority. Mia, for her part, isn't religious. Yet she's one of the few characters here who fully embraces the biblical commandment to love thy neighbor. Photograph: Sergey Kozlov/EPA European Union EU leaders braced for clashes over Ukraine aid at budget talks Slovakia, Hungary and Czechia want to opt out of €45bn Ukraine loan to fill funding black hole caused by Russia’s relentless attacks Europe live – latest updates Jennifer Rankin in Brussels Thu 26 Nov 2026 09.56 EST First published on Thu 26 Nov 2026 07.07 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google EU leaders are bracing for a clash over long-term financial aid for Ukraine amid an effort to finalise high-stakes budget talks by the end of the year. Arriving in Brussels on Thursday, the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz , reiterated his view that all EU member states should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. “When the European Union provides funding, it does so as the European Union – and that union consists of 27 member states, not 23 or 24,” he said. Merz has previously threatened to veto the bloc’s next seven-year budget unless all countries sign up to the Ukraine loan, which would be a painful outcome for member states that are net recipients of EU funds. Slovakia, Hungary and Czechia, net beneficiaries, want to opt out of the loan. Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, who has maintained close ties to the Kremlin , has accused Merz of blackmail. View image in fullscreen From left, France’s Emmanuel Macron, the European Central Bank president, Christine Lagarde, and Germany’s Friedrich Merz, talking in Brussels. Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPA But Bulgaria, which had been against the loan, said on Thursday it was ready to contribute as long as its share was not linked to weapons. “Bulgaria is going to ‌take part in the loan of 20bn [for] non-military support ​for Ukraine,” Bulgaria’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, said as he arrived at the summit. “We have a ⁠huge historic diaspora of Bulgarians living ​in Ukraine. Our wish is ​to concentrate our support ​in that ‌area. We are ​going ​to contribute, but no money from Bulgaria for weapons,” he said. The European Commission last week proposed a €45bn EU loan for Ukraine to fill a funding black hole caused by Russia’s relentless attacks. EU officials proposed €25bn for military spending and €20bn for Ukraine’s civilian needs, such as schools and hospitals. Arriving at the summit, Czechia’s populist prime minister, Andrej Babiš, was in no mood for compromise. “Cohesion is really the goal of the European Union and [the] Czech Republic. We will fight for this money,” he said, referring to the EU’s cohesion funds, which are intended to help poorer regions catch up with richer ones. Babiš said his country needed a highway to Austria and more hospitals. “Financing of Ukraine should be negotiated separately. And the most important is the life of our citizens,” he said, adding that the EU should “do everything” to support peace in Ukraine. But Merz’s stance has won widespread support, especially among western European, Nordic and Baltic states. Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said: “It’s not acceptable to simply kidnap the support for Ukraine by saying that we will accept the European Union support for Ukraine, but we will not pay for it ourselves. That is not a reasonable way of thinking.” However, some governments that support Merz’s goal have reservations about his tactics, fearing the public threat to block cohesion funds could make it harder for recalcitrant governments to climb down. The discussion on support for Ukraine has become entangled in negotiations over the EU’s next long-term budget, which will set the bloc’s spending priorities for 2028-2034. View image in fullscreen Czechia’s populist prime minister, Andrej Babiš, believes financing of Ukraine should be a separate negotiation to the main EU budget. Photograph: Geert Vanden Wijngaert/AP EU leaders are discussing a €1.78tn proposal presented by the European Council president, António Costa, last Saturday, which represents a 10% reduction on the original €2tn plan from the European Commission. EU officials want to finalise a budget deal by the end of the year before a sequence of big elections in 2027 complicates finding an agreement. The far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is the frontrunner in next year’s French presidential elections, wants to slash France’s contribution to the budget and cease funding Ukraine. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion The Irish taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said it was important to get a budget agreement before the end of the year as “the prospects of doing it in the first half of 2027 are very dim”. Separately, Germany is seeking to insulate EU funding for Ukraine from a Le Pen victory: Berlin wants to ensure future decisions on funding Kyiv via the EU budget are made by a majority of EU member states. The current system requires unanimity, enabling one country to veto a decision. Others have pushed back against allowing French elections to dominate the EU budget timetable, and have said making Le Pen the focus gives her ammunition to make a case that the EU is against her political movement. “We should be aware of a self-fulfilling prophecy,” said one senior EU diplomat. “Let’s not be paralysed by elections happening in six months.” Arriving at the summit on Thursday, Costa said all leaders needed to approach discussions with an “open mind, a constructive approach and a sense of compromise” as he called for the budget to be approved in a “timely” way, adding: “That means by the end of this year.” The budget has to be agreed unanimously, but countries are deeply split. In one camp are the so-called frugals – net contributors to the EU budget such as Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden – which want to reduce the overall size and shift spending priorities to defence and competitiveness, rather than farm subsidies and regional funds. In the other camp are 17 countries in southern, central and eastern Europe, which want to ensure the flow of EU funds to traditional policies and oppose cuts. France sits in neither camp, but has vowed to protect the common agriculture policy (CAP), which benefits French farmers. Maintaining farm payments would make it harder for Le Pen to unravel the budget. On the eve of the summit, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said “not a single euro of the CAP must be withheld from France in the next European multi-annual budget”. Le Pen welcomed press reports that Paris was pushing for increased agriculture spending, but said Macron’s position had “nothing to do” with defending French farmers. “The objective would be to dissuade us – if the French entrusted us with the responsibility to govern – from defending French interests in European budgetary negotiations” she wrote on X.
